17 In ages gone an ancient city stood— 18 Carthage, a Tyrian seat, which from afar 19 made front on Italy and on the mouths 20 of Tiber's stream; its wealth and revenues 21 were vast, and ruthless was its quest of war. 22 'T is said that Juno, of all lands she loved, 23 most cherished this,—not Samos' self so dear. 24 Here were her arms, her chariot; even then 25 a throne of power o'er nations near and far, 26 if Fate opposed not, 't was her darling hope 27 to 'stablish here; but anxiously she heard 28 that of the Trojan blood there was a breed 29 then rising, which upon the destined day 30 should utterly o'erwhelm her Tyrian towers, 31 a people of wide sway and conquest proud 32 should compass Libya's doom;—such was the web 33 the Fatal Sisters spun. Such was the fear 34 of Saturn's daughter, who remembered well 35 what long and unavailing strife she waged 36 for her loved Greeks at Troy. Nor did she fail 37 to meditate th' occasions of her rage, 38 and cherish deep within her bosom proud 39 its griefs and wrongs: the choice by Paris made; 40 her scorned and slighted beauty; a whole race 41 rebellious to her godhead; and Jove's smile 42 that beamed on eagle-ravished Ganymede. 43 With all these thoughts infuriate, her power 44 pursued with tempests o'er the boundless main 45 the Trojans, though by Grecian victor spared 46 and fierce Achilles; so she thrust them far 47 from Latium; and they drifted, Heaven-impelled, 48 year after year, o'er many an unknown sea— 49 O labor vast, to found the Roman line! 50 Below th' horizon the Sicilian isle 51 just sank from view, as for the open sea 52 with heart of hope they sailed, and every ship 53 clove with its brazen beak the salt, white waves. 54 But Juno of her everlasting wound 55 knew no surcease, but from her heart of pain 56 thus darkly mused: “Must I, defeated, fail 57 of what I will, nor turn the Teucrian King 58 from Italy away? Can Fate oppose? 59 Had Pallas power to lay waste in flame 60 the Argive fleet and sink its mariners, 61 revenging but the sacrilege obscene 62 by Ajax wrought, Oileus' desperate son? 63 She, from the clouds, herself Jove's lightning threw, 64 scattered the ships, and ploughed the sea with storms. 65 Her foe, from his pierced breast out-breathing fire, 66 in whirlwind on a deadly rock she flung. 67 But I, who move among the gods a queen, 68 Jove's sister and his spouse, with one weak tribe 69 make war so long! Who now on Juno calls? 70 What suppliant gifts henceforth her altars crown?”

71 So, in her fevered heart complaining still, 72 unto the storm-cloud land the goddess came, 73 a region with wild whirlwinds in its womb, 74 Aeolia named, where royal Aeolus 75 in a high-vaulted cavern keeps control 76 o'er warring winds and loud concourse of storms. 77 There closely pent in chains and bastions strong, 78 they, scornful, make the vacant mountain roar, 79 chafing against their bonds. But from a throne 80 of lofty crag, their king with sceptred hand 81 allays their fury and their rage confines. 82 Did he not so, our ocean, earth, and sky 83 were whirled before them through the vast inane. 84 But over-ruling Jove, of this in fear, 85 hid them in dungeon dark: then o'er them piled 86 huge mountains, and ordained a lawful king 87 to hold them in firm sway, or know what time, 88 with Jove's consent, to loose them o'er the world. 89 To him proud Juno thus made lowly plea: 90 “Thou in whose hands the Father of all gods 91 and Sovereign of mankind confides the power 92 to calm the waters or with winds upturn, 93 great Aeolus! a race with me at war 94 now sails the Tuscan main towards Italy, 95 bringing their Ilium and its vanquished powers. 96 Uprouse thy gales. Strike that proud navy down! 97 Hurl far and wide, and strew the waves with dead! 98 Twice seven nymphs are mine, of rarest mould; 99 of whom Deiopea, the most fair, 100 I give thee in true wedlock for thine own, 101 to mate thy noble worth; she at thy side 102 shall pass long, happy years, and fruitful bring 103 her beauteous offspring unto thee their sire.”

104 Then Aeolus: “'T is thy sole task, O Queen, 105 to weigh thy wish and will. My fealty 106 thy high behest obeys. This humble throne 107 is of thy gift. Thy smiles for me obtain 108 authority from Jove. Thy grace concedes 109 my station at your bright Olympian board, 110 and gives me lordship of the darkening storm.” 111 Replying thus, he smote with spear reversed 112 the hollow mountain's wall; then rush the winds 113 through that wide breach in long, embattled line, 114 and sweep tumultuous from land to land: 115 with brooding pinions o'er the waters spread, 116 east wind and south, and boisterous Afric gale 117 upturn the sea; vast billows shoreward roll; 118 the shout of mariners, the creak of cordage, 119 follow the shock; low-hanging clouds conceal 120 from Trojan eyes all sight of heaven and day; 121 night o'er the ocean broods; from sky to sky 122 the thunders roll, the ceaseless lightnings glare; 123 and all things mean swift death for mortal man. 124 Straightway Aeneas, shuddering with amaze, 125 groaned loud, upraised both holy hands to Heaven, 126 and thus did plead: “O thrice and four times blest, 127 ye whom your sires and whom the walls of Troy 128 looked on in your last hour! O bravest son 129 Greece ever bore, Tydides! O that I 130 had fallen on Ilian fields, and given this life 131 struck down by thy strong hand! where by the spear 132 of great Achilles, fiery Hector fell, 133 and huge Sarpedon; where the Simois 134 in furious flood engulfed and whirled away 135 so many helms and shields and heroes slain!”

136 While thus he cried to Heaven, a shrieking blast 137 smote full upon the sail. Up surged the waves 138 to strike the very stars; in fragments flew 139 the shattered oars; the helpless vessel veered 140 and gave her broadside to the roaring flood, 141 where watery mountains rose and burst and fell. 142 Now high in air she hangs, then yawning gulfs 143 lay bare the shoals and sands o'er which she drives. 144 Three ships a whirling south wind snatched and flung 145 on hidden rocks,—altars of sacrifice 146 Italians call them, which lie far from shore 147 a vast ridge in the sea; three ships beside 148 an east wind, blowing landward from the deep, 149 drove on the shallows,—pitiable sight,— 150 and girdled them in walls of drifting sand. 151 That ship, which, with his friend Orontes, bore 152 the Lycian mariners, a great, plunging wave 153 struck straight astern, before Aeneas' eyes. 154 Forward the steersman rolled and o'er the side 155 fell headlong, while three times the circling flood 156 spun the light bark through swift engulfing seas. 157 Look, how the lonely swimmers breast the wave! 158 And on the waste of waters wide are seen 159 weapons of war, spars, planks, and treasures rare, 160 once Ilium's boast, all mingled with the storm. 161 Now o'er Achates and Ilioneus, 162 now o'er the ship of Abas or Aletes, 163 bursts the tempestuous shock; their loosened seams 164 yawn wide and yield the angry wave its will.

165 Meanwhile how all his smitten ocean moaned, 166 and how the tempest's turbulent assault 167 had vexed the stillness of his deepest cave, 168 great Neptune knew; and with indignant mien 169 uplifted o'er the sea his sovereign brow. 170 He saw the Teucrian navy scattered far 171 along the waters; and Aeneas' men 172 o'erwhelmed in mingling shock of wave and sky. 173 Saturnian Juno's vengeful stratagem 174 her brother's royal glance failed not to see; 175 and loud to eastward and to westward calling, 176 he voiced this word:“What pride of birth or power 177 is yours, ye winds, that, reckless of my will, 178 audacious thus, ye ride through earth and heaven, 179 and stir these mountain waves? Such rebels I— 180 nay, first I calm this tumult! But yourselves 181 by heavier chastisement shall expiate 182 hereafter your bold trespass. Haste away 183 and bear your king this word! Not unto him 184 dominion o'er the seas and trident dread, 185 but unto me, Fate gives. Let him possess 186 wild mountain crags, thy favored haunt and home, 187 O Eurus! In his barbarous mansion there, 188 let Aeolus look proud, and play the king 189 in yon close-bounded prison-house of storms!”

211 Aeneas' wave-worn crew now landward made, 212 and took the nearest passage, whither lay 213 the coast of Libya. A haven there 214 walled in by bold sides of a rocky isle, 215 offers a spacious and secure retreat, 216 where every billow from the distant main 217 breaks, and in many a rippling curve retires. 218 Huge crags and two confronted promontories 219 frown heaven-high, beneath whose brows outspread 220 the silent, sheltered waters; on the heights 221 the bright and glimmering foliage seems to show 222 a woodland amphitheatre; and yet higher 223 rises a straight-stemmed grove of dense, dark shade. 224 Fronting on these a grotto may be seen, 225 o'erhung by steep cliffs; from its inmost wall 226 clear springs gush out; and shelving seats it has 227 of unhewn stone, a place the wood-nymphs love. 228 In such a port, a weary ship rides free 229 of weight of firm-fluked anchor or strong chain. 230 Hither Aeneas of his scattered fleet 231 saving but seven, into harbor sailed; 232 with passionate longing for the touch of land, 233 forth leap the Trojans to the welcome shore, 234 and fling their dripping limbs along the ground. 235 Then good Achates smote a flinty stone, 236 secured a flashing spark, heaped on light leaves, 237 and with dry branches nursed the mounting flame. 238 Then Ceres' gift from the corrupting sea 239 they bring away; and wearied utterly 240 ply Ceres' cunning on the rescued corn, 241 and parch in flames, and mill 'twixt two smooth stones. 242 Aeneas meanwhile climbed the cliffs, and searched 243 the wide sea-prospect; haply Antheus there, 244 storm-buffeted, might sail within his ken, 245 with biremes, and his Phrygian mariners, 246 or Capys or Caicus armor-clad, 247 upon a towering deck. No ship is seen; 248 but while he looks, three stags along the shore 249 come straying by, and close behind them comes 250 the whole herd, browsing through the lowland vale 251 in one long line. Aeneas stopped and seized 252 his bow and swift-winged arrows, which his friend, 253 trusty Achates, close beside him bore. 254 His first shafts brought to earth the lordly heads 255 of the high-antlered chiefs; his next assailed 256 the general herd, and drove them one and all 257 in panic through the leafy wood, nor ceased 258 the victory of his bow, till on the ground 259 lay seven huge forms, one gift for every ship. 260 Then back to shore he sped, and to his friends 261 distributed the spoil, with that rare wine 262 which good Acestes while in Sicily 263 had stored in jars, and prince-like sent away 264 with his Ioved guest;—this too Aeneas gave; 265 and with these words their mournful mood consoled.

A sign I tell: 56 Lest thou shouldst deem this message of thy sleep 57 a vain, deluding dream, thou soon shalt find 58 in the oak-copses on my margent green, 59 a huge sow, with her newly-littered brood 60 of thirty young; along the ground she lies, 61 snow-white, and round her udders her white young. 62 There shall thy city stand, and there thy toil 63 shall find untroubled rest. Hard by the city gates 829 the Latins wheeled once more and pressed the rein 830 strong on the yielding neck; the charging foe 831 took flight and hurried far with loose-flung rein. 832 'T was like the shock and onset of the sea 833 that landward hurls the alternating flood 834 and hides high cliffs in foam,—the tawny sands 835 upflinging as it rolls; then, suddenly 836 whirled backward on the reingulfing waves, 837 it quits the ledges, and with ebbing flow 838 far from the shore retires. The Tuscans twice 839 drive back the flying Rutules to the town; 840 and twice repulsed, with shields to rearward thrown, 841 glare back at the pursuer; but conjoined 842 in the third battle-charge, both armies merge 843 confusedly together in grim fight 844 of man to man; then follow dying groans, 845 armor blood-bathed and corpses, and strong steeds 846 inextricably with their masters slain, 847 so fierce the fray.
